There are a few basic ways to add vital dynamics to your model. The simplest is to declare births and deaths for the population, in `demographics=`. `ss.birth(rate=...)` is a crude birth rate (per person per year) of people born into each disease's first state (here `S`), and `ss.death(rate=...)` applies the same death rate to everyone:

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

S, I = ss.states('S I')
sis = ss.Disease(
    infection = ss.Transition(S, I, rate=ss.peryear(2) * I),
    recovery = ss.Transition(I, S, dur=ss.years(1)),
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
demographics = [
    ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)),  # 20 births per 1,000 people per year
    ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.015)), # 15 deaths per 1,000 people per year
]
sim = ss.Sim(sis, demographics=demographics, total_pop=10_000, start='2000', stop='2050')
sim.run()
sim.plot()
```

Births and deaths become flows of the disease like any other transition, so they appear in the results (`sim.results.sis.births`) and in `describe()`. Written this way, the model still runs as an ODE, and with several diseases, the same people are born into and die from each of them, under every solver. The same declaration works as agents, e.g. with a network:

```{python}
pars = dict(
    demographics = [ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.015))],
    networks = 'random',
    diseases = 'sir'
)
sim = ss.Sim(pars)
```

In an agent-based model, births and deaths can also be demographic modules, which add and remove agents, and which take data by year (and, for deaths, by age and sex; below). A rate above 1 is read as per 1,000 people, as crude birth and death rates usually are, and a rate below 1 as per person, so `ss.Births(birth_rate=20)` and `ss.Births(birth_rate=0.02)` are the same. A rate that could be either (from 0.1 to 1, or above 1,000) gives a warning saying which was assumed; `rate_units=1000` (per 1,000) or `rate_units=1` (per person) says which, and silences it:

```{python}
demographics = [
    ss.Births(birth_rate=ss.peryear(20)),
    ss.Deaths(death_rate=ss.peryear(15))
]
sim = ss.Sim(demographics=demographics)
```

You can even simply set `demographics=True` to use default rates (20 births and 10 deaths per 1,000 people per year):

```{python}
ss.Sim(demographics=True).run().plot();
```

By default, agents age if and only if at least one demographics module is included. You can override this behavior by setting `use_aging`, e.g. `ss.Sim(use_aging=False)`

## Scaling results to whole populations
Even though we've been simulating populations of a few thousand agents, we can also use the `total_pop` parameter to scale our results so that they reflect a much larger population. You can think of this as a kind of statistical sampling approximation. If we want to model the population of Nigeria, for example, it would be much too computationally intensive to simulate 200 million agents. However, we could simulate 50,000 agents and then say that each agent represents 4,000 people. Again, we can do this by passing `total_pop=200e6` to the sim or in the `pars` dictionary. Here's an example:

```{python}
demographics = [
    ss.Births(birth_rate=ss.peryear(20)),
    ss.Deaths(death_rate=ss.peryear(15))
]
sim = ss.Sim(pars={'total_pop': 200e6, 'n_agents': 50e3}, demographics=demographics)
```

## Using realistic vital demographics
For more realistic demographics, we can also pass in a file that has birth or death rates over time and by age/sex. There are examples of these files in the `test_data` folder. Here's how we would read them in and construct realistic vital dynamics for Nigeria:

```{python}
import starsim as ss
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Read in age-specific fertility rates
fertility_rates = pd.read_csv('test_data/nigeria_asfr.csv')
pregnancy = ss.Pregnancy(fertility_rate=fertility_rates)

death_rates = pd.read_csv('test_data/nigeria_deaths.csv')
death = ss.Deaths(death_rate=death_rates, rate_units=1)

demographics = [pregnancy, death]

# Make people using the distribution of the population by age/sex in 1995
n_agents = 5_000
nga_pop_1995 = 106819805  # Population of Nigeria in 1995, the year we will start the model
age_data = pd.read_csv('test_data/nigeria_age.csv')
ppl = ss.People(n_agents, age_data=age_data)

# Make the sim, run and plot
sim = ss.Sim(total_pop=nga_pop_1995, start='1995', stop='2030', people=ppl, demographics=demographics, networks='random', diseases='sir')
sim.run()

# Read in a file with the actual population size
nigeria_popsize = pd.read_csv('test_data/nigeria_popsize.csv')
data = nigeria_popsize[(nigeria_popsize.year >= 1995) & (nigeria_popsize.year <= 2030)]

# Plot the overall population size - simulated vs data
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)
res = sim.results
ax.scatter(data.year, data.alive, alpha=0.5, label='Data')
ax.plot(sim.t.yearvec, res.alive, color='k', label='Model')
ax.legend()
ax.set_title('Population')
plt.show()
```

If you want to use realistic demographics for your model, you can adapt the data files and code snippet above to read in the relevant demographic data files for your country/setting. For a country's population size, age structure, and sex ratio, you can also use the data that come with Starsim: `ss.people('Nigeria', year=1995, n_agents=5_000)` in place of `ss.People(...)` (the sim then takes `total_pop` from it too).

*Note*: In the code block above, the mortality data are per person, which we say with `rate_units=1`: the oldest ages have rates above 0.1, which could otherwise be read either way. If your data come in the form of deaths per 1,000 people, set `rate_units=1000`. Note also that as per standard definitions, `fertility_rate` is defined per *woman*, whereas `birth_rate` is defined per *person*.

## Exercises
